forces.title: Public and Private Investment in Digital Infrastructure
forces.description: The UK's computers and telecoms sector benefits from sustained public and private investment in AI, digital infrastructure, and skills development. Initiatives like the Digital and Technologies Sector Plan, AI Growth Zones, and TechFirst are supporting this growth. For fixed line, broadband, and fibre, this translates into increased demand for and investment in core connectivity infrastructure, fostering innovation and expansion. This sustained backing helps to underpin the sector’s long-term strength and resilience against external pressures.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Higher Data-Centre Energy Costs
forces.description: The UK's computers and telecoms sector faces near-term uncertainty due to higher data-centre energy costs. As data centres are integral to the digital infrastructure that fixed line and broadband operators connect to and support, increased energy expenses for these facilities can translate into higher operational costs for telcos or affect the profitability of their data centre clients, potentially impacting revenue streams from connectivity services. This pressure is a significant concern for the sector’s financial flexibility.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Semiconductor Constraints and Supply Chain Volatility
forces.description: Fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators are exposed to near-term uncertainty stemming from semiconductor constraints. Shortages could reduce shipments of critical networking equipment, impacting network build-out, upgrades, and maintenance. This, combined with broader supply-chain pressures, creates volatility in component availability and costs, which can delay projects and compress margins. The challenge requires careful management of supply-chain risks and strategic inventory planning to mitigate disruptions to infrastructure development and service delivery.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Rising Cyber Risks and Major Attacks
forces.description: The telecom sector, including fixed line, broadband, and fibre, faces a critical concern from rising cyber risks, especially following major attacks in 2025. Cybersecurity vulnerabilities can lead to service disruptions, data breaches, and reputational damage. Operators must prioritize robust cybersecurity measures and investments in resilience. These risks create near-term uncertainty and necessitate ongoing vigilance and adaptation of security protocols to protect national communications infrastructure and sensitive data, reinforcing the need for continuous credit assessment.
forces.source_title: September 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: AI Reshaping Telecom Operating Costs and Models
forces.description: Telecom operators are undergoing one of the most significant shifts in operating cost structures in decades, driven by AI integration. As AI agents embed across customer care and network operations, token costs will increasingly comprise 20-30% of operating expenditures, alongside 70-80% traditional opex. This 'agentic operating model' fundamentally alters how fixed line, broadband, and fibre networks are managed, demanding modernization amidst complex legacy systems. The transition is challenging but offers significant value potential if telcos can avoid simply adding AI costs to their existing base without proportional productivity gains.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: Challenges of AI Integration in Telecom
forces.description: Telecom operators face unique complexities in scaling AI, unlike digital-native companies. They must modernize while managing complex legacy operations, business support systems, extensive outsourced workforces, and entrenched vendor relationships. Regulatory and labor constraints further complicate AI integration. This creates a significant risk of 'cost-creep' – higher operating expenses without proportional gains in productivity, customer experience, or growth – if AI is merely bolted onto existing processes rather than driving fundamental transformation. Fixed line and broadband providers must carefully navigate these inherent challenges to realize AI's full potential.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: UK Labour Productivity Boost from AI Adoption
forces.description: AI is expected to significantly boost UK labour productivity by +3.4% over the next decade, one of Europe's strongest gains, contributing +1.7% to GDP. While some roles may be displaced, this broader economic uplift provides a substantial tailwind for the telecom sector, including fixed line and broadband. Operators investing in AI-driven transformation for operational efficiency, network optimization, and new service development can leverage this macro trend to enhance their competitiveness, drive internal productivity improvements, and achieve higher returns on their AI-related investments.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Threat to Telecom Data
forces.description: Quantum technology presents an immediate and substantial challenge for telecom carriers, particularly concerning post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Nation-state actors are actively harvesting encrypted data today, anticipating future decryption capabilities with quantum computers, thereby posing a significant long-term risk to sensitive telecom data. Telcos must prioritize PQC migration across all cryptographic dependencies (e.g., 5G core, RAN, transport, SIM/eSIM infrastructure, VPN, OSS/BSS) to achieve quantum readiness by 2030, a complex and urgent undertaking with regulatory mandates accelerating in Europe.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Quantum Computing for Telecom Optimization Challenges
forces.description: Quantum computing holds significant potential to address complex optimization challenges within the telecom sector, such as network planning, fiber route optimization, RAN optimization (beamforming, interference management), and energy management across cell sites. While production-grade quantum computers are still a few years away (around 2028-2029 for 100 stable logical qubits), carriers need to begin building internal capabilities and selectively exploring high-value use cases now. Early adoption can provide a competitive advantage by potentially resetting industry cost structures and improving efficiency by 30-40%.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Fiber Infrastructure Advantage in Quantum Communications
forces.description: Telecom carriers possess a structural advantage in quantum communications, specifically Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), due to their ownership of extensive fiber infrastructure. QKD offers physics-layer security, complementing post-quantum cryptography, and is commercially viable at metro scale for high-security applications in sectors like government, finance, and healthcare. Piloting QKD in high-value metro segments is a low-regret investment, allowing carriers to build institutional knowledge, test commercial viability, and strategically position themselves for emerging sovereign security propositions, reinforcing their role as trusted infrastructure providers.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Vendor-Dependent PQC Migration Pace Constraints
forces.description: The pace of migration to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for telecom carriers is significantly constrained by the PQC roadmaps and capabilities of equipment vendors (e.g., Ericsson, Nokia). Achieving PQC readiness by the end of 2030 requires coordinated equipment upgrades across the entire network, including 5G core, RAN, transport, and subscriber identity infrastructure. Carriers initiating this work in 2026 are already on the outer edge of a responsible timeline, highlighting that reliance on external vendors can introduce delays and potential vulnerabilities if not managed proactively.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Quantum Readiness as Sovereign Trust Anchor
forces.description: Quantum-safe infrastructure is becoming a prerequisite for carriers positioning themselves as sovereign trust anchors for enterprise AI workloads. Enterprises will not trust their AI data to carriers unable to guarantee quantum-resistant encryption. This elevates quantum readiness, encompassing both post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), from a technical challenge to a strategic differentiator. It reinforces the broader carrier transformation agenda, aligning with autonomous network operations and the compliant delivery demanded by enterprise customers in the AI era.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: AI Reshaping Network Traffic and Demands
forces.description: AI is poised to fundamentally alter telecom networks, moving beyond mere bandwidth consumption to reshape traffic patterns, particularly increasing upstream traffic. It will demand ultra-low latency, edge proximity, enhanced resilience, and dedicated AI data centers. This presents a critical, narrow window of opportunity for fixed line and broadband operators to evolve from being mere capacity providers to core infrastructure enablers for AI. Failure to adapt could relegate them to a commoditized role, highlighting the urgency for strategic investment in AI-ready network capabilities.
forces.source_title: MWC 2026: Telecoms at the Inflection Point

forces.title: Sovereign Digital Infrastructure Opportunity for Telcos
forces.description: The concept of sovereign digital infrastructure presents a significant, largely untapped opportunity for telecom operators, including fixed line and broadband providers. Governments and enterprises increasingly demand secure, local, and reliable infrastructure, often backed by national AI or data center strategies. Telcos, with their control of national infrastructure assets like fiber networks and edge locations, are uniquely positioned to provide the enabling infrastructure and compliance layers. This can drive increased return on invested capital by up to 50% and help them compete with hyperscalers by leveraging trusted local presence and regulatory alignment.
forces.source_title: MWC 2026: Telecoms at the Inflection Point

forces.title: Chip Supply Disruption from AI Data Center Demand
forces.description: The UK's Computers & Telecoms sector faces a significant risk of chip supply disruption in 2026 due to the immense global demand from AI data center projects. This absorption of chip production capacity threatens to impact hardware availability and prices for fixed line, broadband, and fibre network equipment. While the long-term usage of AI in consumer and corporate segments may not sustain very high hardware prices, the near-term risk of temporary shortages could delay network build-outs and upgrades, increasing costs for operators.
forces.source_title: February 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: Reinforced Cybersecurity and Regulatory Investment
forces.description: Recent prominent cyber disruptions have significantly reinforced the need for improved cybersecurity resilience across the telecom sector, particularly impacting smaller firms. Ongoing consultations on telecoms security requirements are expected to drive further investment in robust security measures. For fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators, this structural change means increased capital expenditure on security infrastructure, systems, and compliance. While it poses an operational challenge and cost burden, it also strengthens the sector's long-term integrity and trustworthiness, especially as digital infrastructure becomes more critical.
forces.source_title: February 2026 UK Sector Snippets

forces.title: AI as a Strategic Imperative for Telecom Networks
forces.description: Telecom operators are increasingly viewing AI as a strategic imperative to address structural and cost pressures within their networks. AI is being leveraged to reset network economics, facilitate disciplined growth, and unlock new revenue streams. The goal is to move towards fully autonomous, self-optimizing, and self-healing networks. This foundational shift aims to improve operational efficiency, enhance network performance, and enable differentiated services, marking a significant transformation in how fixed line, broadband, and fibre networks are planned, operated, and monetized.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: AI-driven telecom networks

forces.title: Commoditization of Fibre Broadband Offerings
forces.description: Fibre uptake is contributing to the commoditization of previously premium, gigabit speed offerings within the fixed line and broadband market. Traditional B2C growth engines for telcos are increasingly constrained, with upsell opportunities diminishing as high-speed internet becomes a standard expectation. This reduces pricing power and profit margins. Alongside fixed-mobile convergence saturation and declining linear TV viewership, operators are compelled to seek growth 'beyond the core' by diversifying into adjacent services, as relying solely on connectivity for revenue growth is becoming unsustainable.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: B2C growth beyond the core

forces.title: Telcos as Core AI Infrastructure Backbone Enablers
forces.description: Telecom operators, particularly fixed line and broadband providers, have a significant opportunity to reignite growth by playing a major role in the AI infrastructure value chain. They possess crucial assets like extensive fiber networks, national footprints, edge presence, and power access, which are essential for training, deploying, and scaling AI workloads. By leveraging these existing assets and experience in managing complex, high-availability networks, telcos can transition from being mere connectivity providers to core enablers of the AI era, thus capturing a greater share of the economic value generated by technological advancements.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: AI infrastructure

forces.title: LEO Satellite Impact on Fixed Broadband Edges
forces.description: Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellites are emerging as a complementary technology that will reset customer connectivity expectations at the 'edges' of fixed and mobile networks. LEO capacity expansion is enabling it to push into suburban markets, selectively discounting to win market share, and making 'served-on-paper' broadband (e.g., congested FWA, copper-based infrastructure) particularly vulnerable. While not a direct replacement for terrestrial fixed networks, LEO introduces new strategic uncertainty and competition, compelling fixed line and broadband operators to refine their strategies on where to compete, partner, or ignore this evolving market segment.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Satellite connectivity

forces.title: Fiber Networks as Future-Proof Wireline Backbone
forces.description: Fiber networks have cemented their role as the future-proof wireline technology, replacing copper as the backbone for fixed broadband, mobile backhaul, enterprise connectivity, and long-haul connectivity. This structural shift provides stable, infrastructure-like returns for operators. However, as fiber coverage expands and markets mature, challenges in maintaining utilization growth and slower rollout rates emerge. Future value creation will require moving beyond passive ownership to reposition fiber infrastructure as dynamic platforms at the center of the digital economy, emphasizing take-up, service expansion, and efficiency.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Telecom infrastructure

forces.title: Slowing Fibre Deal Activity and Multiples
forces.description: Fibre deal multiples have experienced a modest decline, dropping from 20 times EBITDA in 2022 to approximately 19 times in 2025. Concurrently, fiber deal activity has slowed significantly, with an annual reduction of 20% between 2022 and 2025. This indicates a cyclical weakening in the market for fiber infrastructure assets, as owners are reluctant to sell at lower valuations, leading to longer holding periods. This trend reflects market maturity and slower organic growth in fiber rollout, impacting investment and consolidation strategies for fixed line and broadband providers.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Telecom infrastructure

forces.title: AI Data Center Investment Driving Fibre Demand
forces.description: Massive investment in data centers to support AI workloads is fundamentally reshaping and accelerating fiber demand. Grid power constraints in primary hubs are spurring new subsea, long-haul, and metro fiber builds, specifically targeting secondary markets and Tier-2 cities with available compute capacity. This creates a significant tailwind for fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators, as the need for high-capacity, low-latency connectivity to these expanding data centers drives new construction and enhances the value of existing fiber assets. The accelerating race to build AI-driven data center infrastructure translates directly into increased demand for fiber.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Telecom infrastructure

forces.title: LEO Satellite Competition for Fibre Addressable Market
forces.description: Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellites are emerging as a complementary, not substitutive, technology to fiber, but pose a competitive risk to fixed line and broadband providers. Executives anticipate LEO to capture approximately 20% of existing fiber's addressable market, especially in hard-to-reach areas where terrestrial build-out is uneconomical. This reinforces a hybrid connectivity model, potentially limiting fiber's expansion into underserved segments and pressuring take-up rates in certain geographies. Fixed line operators must strategize to integrate or compete with LEO solutions to maintain market share and profitability.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Telecom infrastructure

forces.title: AI for Value-Led Network Planning Optimization
forces.description: AI is transforming network planning for telecom operators, moving from static engineering thresholds to value-based optimization. Advanced machine learning models and digital twins simulate thousands of rollout and upgrade scenarios, considering impacts on customer experience, traffic evolution, churn, and ARPU. Operators deploying AI-based planning engines report 10-20% lower greenfield rollout capex, 15-35% lower upgrade capex, and reallocation of 20-30% of annual capex from low-ROI interventions. This represents a significant upside for fixed line and broadband providers to enhance efficiency and make more disciplined investment decisions.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: AI-driven telecom networks

forces.title: Value Shift to 'Ready' Assets for AI Infrastructure
forces.description: Grid power limitations and protracted permitting timelines are slowing the construction of new AI data centers, consequently increasing the value of existing infrastructure with available power and space. This dynamic acts as a tailwind for fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators who control 'ready' assets – particularly sites with assured, contracted power in locations capable of supporting distributed compute for AI inference workloads. These assets, such as central offices or edge locations, become strategically valuable, offering telcos an advantage in the race to provide critical AI infrastructure by enabling faster deployment and avoiding common build-out bottlenecks.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: AI infrastructure

forces.title: Satellite Competition Driving ARPU Compression
forces.description: The scaling of Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellite capacity and intensifying competition risk anchoring lower price expectations, leading to ARPU compression in competitive, non-fiber broadband technologies. As LEO providers selectively discount prices to fill beam capacity and win market share, it could exert downward pressure on pricing norms for traditional fixed line and broadband services, particularly in areas with existing congestion or copper-based infrastructure. This force represents a direct challenge to the profitability and revenue growth of incumbent fixed line operators, compelling them to adapt their pricing strategies and service offerings.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Satellite connectivity

forces.title: High Capital Needs and Pricing Pressure in AI Infrastructure
forces.description: Investing in AI-ready infrastructure, including GPU-as-a-service (GPUaaS), dark fiber, and AI-ready data centers, demands significant capital expenditure from fixed line and broadband operators. This is compounded by short technology cycles, requiring continuous investment to stay competitive. Furthermore, as supply expands in these areas, pricing pressure could intensify, potentially compressing margins and impacting returns on these substantial investments. Many telcos also lack the requisite software, sales, and partnership capabilities, increasing the execution risk and challenging their ability to compete effectively against hyperscalers with superior scale and capital.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: AI infrastructure

forces.title: Low Fibre Take-Up Rates and Overlapping Networks
forces.description: Fixed line and broadband fiber networks, particularly consumer-focused builds, face significant challenges from low take-up rates, often falling below the 30% threshold needed for sustainable profitability. This issue is exacerbated by network overbuilding, where multiple providers deploy fiber in the same areas, leading to increased competition and fragmented customer bases. The slow migration from legacy copper infrastructure further prolongs the period where new fiber investments struggle to achieve optimal utilization. These factors combine to put pressure on revenue growth and profitability for fiber operators.
forces.source_title: Issue Brief: Telecom infrastructure

forces.title: Completion of Major Fibre Rollouts
forces.description: Many costly fiber rollouts are nearing completion, indicating a potential deceleration in investment capital growth for fixed line and broadband operators. After a period of significant infrastructure build-out, the industry is adopting a more hesitant, 'wait-and-see' approach to further capital outlays. While this suggests a shift from heavy capex cycles, it also implies a need for operators to focus on monetizing existing assets and extracting value from their extensive fiber footprints rather than relying on new build expansion for growth. This is a cyclical shift from deployment to optimization.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: AI for Significant Cost Reduction in Operations
forces.description: AI-driven cost efficiency is a foundational element of telecom transformation. Harnessing AI to redesign processes across all operations and support functions, from procurement to financial planning, can lead to significant cost reductions. Examples include Telstra's AU $122 million savings by embedding AI in corporate processes and a telco's financial planning team saving millions by automating data collection. For fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators, this means optimizing network operations, customer care, and back-office functions, leading to improved profitability and a more agile operating model.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: AI-Enabled Zero-Touch Autonomous Operations
forces.description: Fixed line and broadband operators can achieve significant efficiency gains through AI-enabled zero-touch operations, minimizing human intervention across functions. The goal of proactive, autonomous operations has the potential to radically reshape back-office and support functions, requiring seamless, real-time cross-domain data flows linking IT, network, and operations. This transformation allows for automated tendering, supplier onboarding, spend analysis, and proactive fault management, leading to improved decision-making, reduced operating expenses (e.g., up to 30% reduction in network opex), and enhanced network resilience and performance.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: Expansion into Vertical Ecosystems for New Revenue
forces.description: To combat commoditization of core connectivity, fixed line and broadband operators are expanding into vertical ecosystems, offering adjacent services like security, entertainment, insurance, energy, and fintech. This strategy leverages their extensive reach and infrastructure to unlock new revenue pools and deepen customer relationships. Examples include MasOrange's success in energy and insurance, and Telus deriving a quarter of its revenue from B2B digital verticals. This shift from selling discrete products to delivering integrated, value-added services is critical for sustainable growth, ARPU uplift, and churn reduction, moving towards a more resilient value creation model.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: Growth in B2B ICT Products and Services
forces.description: Fixed line and broadband operators have a lucrative opportunity to expand their B2B offerings into end-to-end ICT solutions, including cloud, cybersecurity, and IT managed services. This diversification responds to enterprises seeking third-party support for optimizing complex technologies. This dynamic business segment can contribute up to 20% of total telco revenue. Success requires upgrading infrastructure, upskilling employees, and forging key partnerships, enabling telcos to move beyond core connectivity to provide higher-value enterprise services and capitalize on digital transformation trends within their business customer base.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: Network APIs for 5G Monetization
forces.description: The monetization of 5G has been challenging for telcos, but standardized, global API platforms for network capabilities present a significant upside. These APIs enable the creation of new 5G-related products and services, leveraging features like speed on demand, low-latency connections, speed tiering, and edge compute discovery. Fixed line and broadband operators, as providers of underlying fiber backhaul for 5G, can play a crucial role in enabling these platforms, generating incremental revenue and facilitating innovative B2B and B2C offerings. Examples like the Brazilian operators' fraud prevention APIs show tangible revenue and consumer benefits.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: Private 5G Networks for Enterprise Monetization
forces.description: Private 5G networks offer a significant vehicle for fixed line and broadband operators to increase their return on 5G investments through customized, vertical-specific enterprise architecture. These specialized networks enable advanced use cases in sectors like logistics, manufacturing, public sector, smart hospitals, and augmented retail. By providing reliable, enterprise-grade wireless spectrum access, often in partnership with industrial players or hyperscalers, telcos can fuel incremental 5G monetization opportunities. This expands their role beyond public network provision to become crucial enablers of digital transformation for specific industries.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

forces.title: AI and Automation for Network Excellence
forces.description: Network quality is reemerging as a key differentiator for fixed line, broadband, and fibre operators as AI workloads and digital services shift to the edge. Incorporating AI and automation throughout the network lifecycle—from planning, construction, and deployment to fault management and inventory—enables operators to deliver intelligent, high-performing, and resilient networks. This approach can significantly reduce network operating expenses by up to 30% and total capital expenses by as much as 15%, transforming networks from mere technical assets into key drivers of value creation and competitive advantage.
forces.source_title: The telco reinvention: How AI can fuel value creation

viewpoints.title: UK Computers & Telecoms Sector Resilient with Digital Infrastructure Investment
viewpoints.description: The UK computers and telecoms sector shows resilience despite geopolitical, energy, and supply-chain challenges. Sustained public and private investment in AI and digital infrastructure, including initiatives like the Digital and Technologies Sector Plan, underpins its long-term strength. However, the sector faces near-term uncertainties from elevated data-centre energy costs, semiconductor shortages, and increasing cyber risks. Businesses are advised to manage energy, cyber, supply-chain, and workforce risks carefully, while leveraging AI and connectivity opportunities. The overall outlook is cautiously positive, but credit assessment remains prudent.

viewpoints.title: UK Computers & Telecoms: Policy Backing Amid Chip & Cyber Risks
viewpoints.description: The UK Computers & Telecoms sector benefits from sustained government policy support and robust structural demand for digital capabilities. This includes rising public R&D funding and digital skills initiatives, notably the Vodafone–Three UK merger signifying major development. However, the sector faces risks from chip supply disruptions due to AI data center demand, which could impact production and prices in 2026. Cybersecurity, data protection, and evolving regulatory frameworks are defining themes. The outlook is cautiously positive, but resilience against supply chain and cyber threats is paramount, particularly for fixed line and broadband infrastructure.

demand_drivers.description: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data centers in both core and Tier 2 cities creates demand for high-capacity fiber connectivity.
Hyperscalers and colocation providers increasingly prefer dark fiber for their new data centers, representing a specific and high-value demand segment.

new_opportunities.description: Telcos can monetize their fiber assets by providing high-capacity, low-latency, and dark fiber connections to the rapidly expanding AI data center ecosystem, capturing a significant revenue pool.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Fiber Connectivity to AI Data Centers

market_sizing.methodology: Forecast of global revenue opportunity for fiber connectivity specifically for new data centers in core and Tier 2 cities. The range is $30 billion to $50 billion, driven by the requirement for high-capacity, often dark-fiber, connections to these new facilities.

pnl_drivers.description: High annual egress costs ($70-80 billion) create a market for telcos to offer intelligent network services that help enterprises manage AI workloads, control costs, and meet latency/regulatory requirements, improving telco revenue.

new_opportunities.description: Telcos can offer software-defined network services to enterprises to manage AI workloads, reduce cloud data transfer fees (egress costs), and meet latency/regulatory requirements, creating a new revenue stream.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Intelligent Network Services for Cloud Egress

market_sizing.methodology: Annual estimate of global cloud data transfer (egress) fees, stated as $70 billion to $80 billion. This figure highlights the scope for telcos to offer differentiated intelligent, software-defined network services.

demand_drivers.description: Rapid growth of accelerated compute workloads (over 30% CAGR) requiring specialized GPU resources, comprising over two-thirds of future data center demand.
Increasing demand for distributed compute closer to end-users, where telcos can utilize existing space, power, and cooling assets.

new_opportunities.description: Telcos can repurpose central offices or spaces with power/cooling to offer GPUaaS, participating in a $35-70 billion market by 2030 for distributed compute for AI workloads.

market_sizing.methodology: Forecast of the global GPU-as-a-service (GPUaaS) market value by 2030, excluding hyperscalers. The market is driven by accelerated compute workloads, growing at over 30% CAGR and expected to comprise more than two-thirds of data center demand within five years. The market is estimated to be worth $35 billion to $70 billion.
